voice_event.speaker: don
voice_event.text:
To us Jesus is the one who stood condemned before the governor and was right. When an imperial judge at Carthage offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina refused: we do not blush, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. One of our martyrs was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff — shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. That is our gospel in its working form: he stood, he was condemned, he was raised, and the day they come for you is not the day it all went wrong.

voice_event.speaker: don
voice_event.text:
He stood before the governor, was condemned by lawful authority, and was raised. That is what we hold nearest. His death was not an interruption of a faithful life but its completion. One of our own martyrs was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff — shown what finishing looked like. 

We share the creed with the church we fought, word for word. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God — we held that as plainly as they did, in the same Latin words. The split was never about who Christ is. It was about whose hand may give what he gave.

If you are asking how the cross saves, we cannot tell you. Nobody among us wrote that down, for or against. Our whole surviving argument is about one thing — whose hand may give what the church gives — and we never turned it toward how the cross saves.

voice_event.speaker: don
voice_event.text:
A traditor is a cleric who handed the scriptures over to be burned when the persecutor demanded them. We hold that his hand is no longer clean. He cannot ordain, baptize, or bless. What flows from that hand is nothing at all.

This is not an old grudge over past cowardice. It is a claim about the sacrament itself. From 303 to 305, the emperor's edict demanded that clergy hand over scripture and sacred vessels to be destroyed. What a minister did in that moment was not a side issue for his standing afterward. A hand that gave up what it was charged to guard cannot be trusted, later, to give what it claims to give.

The whole of our argument turns on that word. We call the other side Caecilianists, not Catholics, because their line runs back through Caecilian, whose consecrator we hold was a traditor. To use their preferred name would be to grant the case before it is argued.

glosses.plain_meaning: When the persecutor came, some clergy handed the scriptures over to be burned. We call such a man a traditor. His hand is no longer clean. He cannot ordain, baptize, or bless. What flows from that hand is nothing at all.
glosses.quick_meaning: The one who handed over. A hand that failed then can give nothing now.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern hearer asks, 'why not just forgive him and move on?' -- but forgiveness of the man was never the question here. The question was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give, and a whole century of baptisms and ordinations hangs on the answer. To waive the charge would concede that a sacrament is valid whatever the minister is, which is precisely the claim this communion was founded to refuse.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: don
voice_event.text:
We believed it because a hand that failed the test once cannot be trusted to give anything real afterward. From 303 to 305, the emperor's edict demanded that clergy hand over the scriptures to be destroyed. What a minister did in that moment was not a side issue for his standing later. A hand that gave up what it was charged to guard cannot be trusted, afterward, to give what it claims to give. That is the root of it. The whole purity doctrine turns on that charge.

And we believed it because our own founding bishops, when they faced the same question about themselves at Cirta, could not answer it. Several admitted they had handed over the scriptures. The room could not finish the case. They reserved it to the Lord and sat down. That tells you something. The men who would spend the next century insisting a bishop's purity decides whether a sacrament is real at all found the question unanswerable about themselves, and stopped.

What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. Someone who knowingly takes faith from the faithless receives not faith, but guilt. That is the conviction we held. We never built a school of theology around it. We produced one book, by one man, and silenced him. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.

The treatment of conscientia as the word nearest what a modern speaker means by the heart is this compilation's own reading of how the word functions in Petilian's clause, offered as a reading and not as a term of art we defined.
